lessons.title: Determining Harvest Maturity
lessons.body: Harvesting citrus at the right time is critical for taste, shelf life, and market price. In Africa, most citrus is harvested by hand, so you must know when to start. The easiest test is colour: for oranges, the skin should change from green to a uniform orange or yellow-orange. But colour alone can fool youâsome varieties stay green even when ripe. A more reliable method is the Brix test. Use a refractometer (costs about $20) to measure sugar content. For oranges, aim for 10-12% Brix; for lemons, 7-8%. Also check acidity with a simple acid test kit. The ratio of Brix to acid should be at least 8:1 for sweet oranges. Another field test: pick a fruit and taste it. If it's sweet and juicy, it's ready. For export, you also need to check firmnessâsoft fruit bruises easily. Walk your orchard every 3 days as harvest approaches. In Kenya, for example, Valencia oranges are ready 8-10 months after flowering. Don't harvest too earlyâimmature fruit shrivels and lacks juice. Don't wait too longâoverripe fruit drops and rots. Start with a small test pick, then harvest the whole block within a week.

lessons.title: Harvesting Techniques and Tools
lessons.body: How you pick citrus affects how long it lasts. Always use sharp, clean tools. The best tool is a pair of curved harvesting snips (also called clippers). They cost about $10-15. Never pull fruit off the treeâthat tears the skin and leaves a wound where rot enters. Instead, cut the stem close to the fruit, leaving a tiny button (about 2mm). For high branches, use a pole pruner with a basket to catch fruit. Wear soft cotton gloves to avoid scratching the peel. Harvest in the cool of the dayâearly morning or late afternoon. Never harvest wet fruit; wait until dew dries. Work from the outside of the tree inward, and from bottom to top. Place fruit gently into a picking bag or a plastic bucket lined with a soft cloth. Don't drop fruit into the bucketâeach drop causes bruising that shows up later as brown spots. In South Africa, commercial farms use picking bags with a strap over the shoulder and a false bottom to empty fruit slowly into bins. For smallholders, a 20-litre bucket works fine. Do not throw fruit into a pile. After picking, move fruit to shade immediately. A tree can yield 50-100 kg of fruit per season, so plan your labour. One picker can harvest about 200-300 kg per day if fruit is easy to reach.

lessons.title: Field Handling and Transport
lessons.body: Once picked, citrus starts to lose quality. Field heat is the enemy. Move fruit to a shady area within 30 minutes. Never leave fruit in the sunâtemperatures above 30Â°C cause rapid water loss and sunburn. Use clean plastic crates (not sacks) for transport. Sacks crush fruit and cause bruising. A standard crate holds 15-20 kg. Stack crates no more than 5 high to avoid crushing the bottom layer. If you use a pickup truck, cover the load with a white tarpaulin to reflect heat. Avoid driving on rough roadsâvibration causes internal damage. For long distances (over 2 hours), use a refrigerated truck if possible, but if not, transport at night when it's cooler. In many African countries, farmers lose 20-30% of fruit due to poor transport. To reduce losses, harvest only what you can transport within 4 hours. If you must store fruit overnight in the field, put it in a ventilated shed, not a closed room. Never mix fruit from different trees or different maturity stagesâone rotten fruit can spoil the whole batch. Before loading, sort out any fruit with cuts, soft spots, or signs of decay. Feed those to animals or process them immediately. Clean your crates after every use with soap and water, then dry them in the sun. Dirty crates carry fungal spores that cause blue and green mould.

lessons.title: Packinghouse Operations and Grading
lessons.body: A packinghouse is where fruit is cleaned, graded, and packed for market. Even a smallholder can set up a simple shed with a concrete floor, a water tank, and sorting tables. First, dump fruit gently into a water bath with a mild detergent (2 ml per litre) to remove dust and insects. Do not soak for more than 2 minutes. Then rinse with clean water. Next, dry the fruit with a soft cloth or a fan. Grading is sorting by size, colour, and quality. Use a sizing ring or a simple wooden gauge. For oranges, sizes are: small (60-65 mm), medium (65-72 mm), large (72-80 mm), and jumbo (over 80 mm). Remove all fruit with blemishes, soft spots, or green patches. These go to juice or animal feed. For export, you must also wax the fruit to slow water loss. Food-grade wax (carnauba or shellac) costs about $5 per litre and covers 200 kg of fruit. Apply a thin coat with a soft brush or sponge. Then pack into clean, ventilated cartons. Each carton holds 15 kg or 18 kg. Label with variety, size, and farm name. In Kenya, a 15-kg carton of export-quality oranges can fetch $10-15, while ungraded fruit sells for $3-5. Proper grading can double your income. Always keep records of how many cartons you pack per day.

lessons.title: Storage Conditions and Shelf Life
lessons.body: Citrus can be stored for weeks if you control temperature and humidity. The ideal storage for oranges and lemons is 5-8Â°C with 85-90% relative humidity. For limes, 10-12Â°C. If you don't have a cold room, you can use a charcoal coolerâa simple structure with wet charcoal walls and a fan. This can keep fruit at 10-15Â°C in hot climates. Never store citrus with apples, bananas, or tomatoesâthese produce ethylene gas that speeds up ripening and decay. Also, keep fruit away from onions and potatoes; they absorb odours. In a well-ventilated room, citrus can last 2-3 weeks. In a cold room, 6-8 weeks. Check stored fruit every 3 days. Remove any fruit that shows soft spots or mould. One rotten fruit can spread spores to the whole box. For small quantities, you can store in a clean plastic bag with holes (to allow air) in the bottom of a refrigerator. But do not wash fruit before storageâmoisture encourages mould. If you sell at local markets, harvest only what you can sell in 5 days. For longer storage, consider processing. Remember: shelf life depends on how you handled fruit in the field. Bruised fruit will rot first. So always handle gently from tree to store.

lessons.title: Value-Added Processing (Juice, Marmalade, etc.)
lessons.body: Processing turns low-grade or surplus citrus into higher-value products. Juice is the easiest. You need a manual or electric juicer. For 10 kg of oranges, you get about 5 litres of juice. Pasteurize by heating to 80Â°C for 15 minutes, then bottle in clean glass bottles. Add 1 teaspoon of citric acid per litre to preserve colour. Juice can be sold fresh or frozen. Marmalade is made from the peel and pulp. Use equal weights of fruit and sugar. Slice fruit thinly, soak overnight in water, then boil with sugar until it sets (about 105Â°C). Pour into sterilized jars. A 500g jar sells for $3-5 in local markets. Dried peel is another product: dry orange peel in the sun for 3-4 days, then grind into powder for baking or tea. Citrus essential oil can be extracted by cold pressing the peel, but this requires a press. For small-scale, focus on juice and marmalade. In Nigeria, women's groups process citrus into juice and marmalade and sell to supermarkets. You need a food-grade kitchen, clean water, and proper labelling. Always check local food safety regulations. Processing also reduces wasteâfruit that is too small or blemished can still be used. Start small: process 20 kg per day, test the market, then scale up.

quiz.q: What is the recommended Brix level for ripe oranges?
quiz.explanation: Oranges are considered mature when Brix is between 10-12%.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for harvesting citrus?
quiz.explanation: Curved snips cut the stem cleanly without damaging the fruit.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pulling fruit off the tree?
options: B) It tears the skin and invites rot
C) It reduces next year's yield
quiz.explanation: Tearing the skin creates a wound where fungi can enter.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time fruit should be left in the sun after picking?
quiz.explanation: Field heat causes rapid quality loss; move to shade within 30 minutes.

quiz.q: Which container is best for transporting citrus?
quiz.explanation: Plastic crates protect fruit from crushing and allow ventilation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for oranges?
quiz.explanation: Oranges store best at 5-8Â°C with high humidity.

quiz.q: Which fruit should never be stored with citrus?
quiz.explanation: Apples produce ethylene gas that speeds up citrus decay.

quiz.q: What is the first step in packinghouse operations?
quiz.explanation: Washing removes dust and insects before further handling.

quiz.q: What does a refractometer measure?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix, which indicates sugar level.

quiz.q: How long can citrus last in a charcoal cooler?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal coolers keep fruit at 10-15Â°C, extending life to 2-3 weeks.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of post-harvest losses in African citrus?
quiz.explanation: Rough transport and lack of shade cause 20-30% losses.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to cut citrus from the tree?
options: B) Cut stem close to fruit
quiz.explanation: Cutting the stem close to the fruit leaves a small button and avoids skin damage.

quiz.q: Which size of orange is considered 'large'?
quiz.explanation: Large oranges are 72-80 mm in diameter.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of waxing citrus?
quiz.explanation: Wax creates a barrier that reduces moisture loss and extends shelf life.

quiz.q: How much juice can you get from 10 kg of oranges?
quiz.explanation: Oranges yield about 50% juice by weight, so 10 kg gives 5 litres.

quiz.q: What temperature is used to pasteurize citrus juice?
quiz.explanation: Heating to 80Â°C for 15 minutes kills spoilage organisms.

quiz.q: What is the ideal Brix-to-acid ratio for sweet oranges?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of at least 8:1 ensures good sweetness.

quiz.q: Why should you not wash fruit before storage?
quiz.explanation: Wet fruit is more prone to fungal growth during storage.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of maturity in oranges?
quiz.explanation: Colour change from green to orange is the first visual indicator.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored citrus?
quiz.explanation: Checking every 3 days allows you to remove rotting fruit before it spreads.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of grading fruit?
quiz.explanation: Graded fruit fetches higher prices, often double that of ungraded.

quiz.q: Which of these is a value-added citrus product?
quiz.explanation: Marmalade is processed from citrus and sells at a higher value.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of detergent for washing citrus?
quiz.explanation: A mild solution of 2 ml per litre is enough to clean without damaging fruit.

quiz.q: Why should you harvest in the cool of the day?
quiz.explanation: Cool temperatures reduce field heat and water loss.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for citrus storage?
quiz.explanation: High humidity prevents shriveling and weight loss.

quiz.q: How many crates high should you stack citrus?
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 5 high can crush the bottom crates.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of blue and green mould?
quiz.explanation: Fungal spores survive on dirty crates and infect fruit.

quiz.q: Which citrus type stores best at 10-12Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Limes are more sensitive to cold and store best at 10-12Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for maturity without a refractometer?
quiz.explanation: Tasting a sample fruit gives a good indication of sweetness and ripeness.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove rotten fruit from storage?
options: B) To prevent spread of mould
quiz.explanation: One rotten fruit can spread spores and spoil the whole batch.
